'''Arthur Bertram Cuthbert Walker Jr.''' (August 24, 1936 – April 29, 2001) was an American [[solar physicist]] and a pioneer of [[ultraviolet|EUV/XUV]] optics.  He developed [[normal incidence]] [[multilayer optics|multilayer]] XUV [[telescopes]] to photograph the [[solar corona]].  Two of his sounding rocket payloads, the [[Stanford]]/[[Marshall Space Flight Center|MSFC]] Rocket [[Spectroheliograph]] Experiment and the [[MSSTA|Multi-Spectral Solar Telescope Array]], recorded the first full-disk, high-resolution images of the [[Sun]] in XUV with conventional geometries of normal incidence optics. This technology is used in solar telescopes such as [[Solar and Heliospheric Observatory|SOHO/EIT]] and [[TRACE]], and in the fabrication of [[Integrated circuit|microchips]] via [[ultraviolet]] [[photolithography]].

==Early life and education==
Walker was born in [[Cleveland, Ohio]] on August 24, 1936, to Arthur and Hilda Walker.<ref name=nytimes_20010509>James Glanz, [https://www.nytimes.com/2001/05/09/us/arthur-walker-64-scientist-and-mentor-dies.html Arthur Walker, 64, Scientist and Mentor, Dies], ''[[The New York Times]]'' (May 9, 2001).</ref>  He was an only child.<ref name=stanford-report_2001004>Dawn Levy, [http://news.stanford.edu/news/2000/october4/walkerprofile-104.html Art Walter: 'favorite sun' of solar physics], ''Stanford Report'' (October 4, 2000).</ref> Arthur moved to [[New York City]] at the age of five. Arthur attended [[Bronx High School of Science]].<ref name=":02" /> In 1957 he completed his undergraduate studies at [[Case Institute of Technology]] in Cleveland. Here, he earned his bachelor's degree in physics.<ref name=":02" />

Both his master's degree and doctorate in [[astrophysics]] came from the [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign|University of Illinois]], in 1958 and 1962 respectively.<ref name=":123">{{Cite web|url=http://www.math.buffalo.edu/mad/physics/walker_arthurbc.html|title=Arthur Bertram Cuthbert Walker, Jr.|last=Williams|first=Scott|date=2008|website=math.buffalo.edu|access-date=December 4, 2017}}</ref> His dissertation for his doctorate titled, “[[Photo-meson|Photo meson]] Production from Neutrons Bound in Helium and Deuterium,”<ref name=":2" /> focused on the atomic binding of protons and neutrons, as well as the radiation and force carriers involved in this process.<ref name=":123"/>

==Career==
In 1962, Walker began his scientific career in the [[U.S. Air Force]]. He held the rank of first lieutenant, and worked in the Weapons Laboratory. Walker helped to create a satellite to study [[Van Allen radiation belt|Van Allen belt radiation]].<ref name=":123"/>

He also worked at the [[Space physics|Space Physics]] Laboratory of the [[Aerospace Corporation]], when his military stint ended in 1965.<ref name=":123"/> Here, Walker directed the Space Astronomy Program from 1971 to 1973.<ref name=":03">{{Cite web|url=https://news.stanford.edu/news/2005/may18/memlwalk-051805.html|title=Memorial Resolution: Arthur B.C. Walker, Jr.|last=Petrosian|first=Vahe|date=May 18, 2005|website=news.stanford.edu|access-date=December 4, 2017}}</ref> Much of his career involved using rocket technology and satellites to study the Sun's atmosphere at the ultraviolet and X-ray levels.<ref name=":02" />

He was a [[professor]] at [[Stanford University]] from 1974 until his death on April 29, 2001. Walker started as the associate professor of applied physics in January 1974 and became a full professor in 1982. By 1991 he became a joint professor in applied physics and physics.<ref name=":123"/> Walker was a member of the Stanford's Center for Space and Astrophysics, as well as the Astronomy Program, for all his time at the school. He also chaired the Astronomy Program from 1977 to 1980.<ref name=":03" />

Walker mentored thirteen graduate students over his career at Stanford, and a majority of these students came from underrepresented groups in science.<ref name=":02" /> His first graduate student, [[Sally Ride]], went on to become the first American woman in space.<ref name=":13">{{Cite news|url=http://www.skyandtelescope.com/astronomy-resources/famous-astronomers/arthur-b-c-walker-ii-x-ray-astrophysicist/|title=Arthur B. C. Walker II: X-ray Astrophysicist – Sky & Telescope|last=Aceves|first=Ana|date=August 4, 2016|work=Sky & Telescope|access-date=December 24, 2017|language=en-US}}</ref>  Walker also set up an informal advocacy association with other black faculty members called the "[[Benjamin Banneker|Banneker]] Group".<ref name="stanford-report_2001004" />

He was instrumental in building Congressional approval for the [[National Solar Observatory]], and served on the [[Rogers Commission]] which investigated the explosion of the [[Space Shuttle Challenger|Space Shuttle ''Challenger'']] in 1986.<ref name=":13" />

== Research ==
Walker, alongside H.R. Rugge, completed early studies, from 1965 to 1975, to view the Sun's atmosphere with X-ray imaging.<ref name=":123"/> After coming to Stanford, Walker began working with Troy Barbee of the school's Material Sciences Department to observe the Sun's corona.<ref name=":02">{{Cite web|last=Petrosian|first=Vahé|date=December 2001|title=Arthur B. C. Walker (1936–2001)|url=https://aas.org/obituaries/arthur-b-c-walker-1936-2001|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130826152433/https://aas.org/obituaries/arthur-b-c-walker-1936-2001|archive-date=August 26, 2013|access-date=April 22, 2021|website=American Astronomical Society}}</ref> Walker believed that Barbee's multilayered thin films would provide improved images for an X-ray telescope.<ref name=":02" /> In 1987, Barbee and Walker's satellites captured some of the first images of the Sun's corona.<ref name=":02" />

Before his death, Walker was researching X-ray spectroscopy technology. He and his colleagues used this technology to develop three-dimensional images of celestial objects.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=http://www.blackpast.org/aaw/walker-arthur-bertram-cuthbert-jr-1936-2001|title=Walker, Arthur Bertram Cuthbert, Jr. (1936–2001) {{!}} The Black Past: Remembered and Reclaimed|last=Fikes|first=Robert|website=www.blackpast.org|language=en|access-date=December 24, 2017}}</ref> This new technology was the basis of the dark matter detection method advanced by Professor [[Blas Cabrera Navarro|Blas Cabrera]] of Stanford's physics department.<ref name=":02" />

==Death and legacy==
Walker died on April 29, 2001, at home on the Stanford campus, following a battle with cancer.<ref name=stanford-report_20010502>Dawn Levy, [http://news.stanford.edu/news/2001/may2/walkerobit-52.html Solar physicist Art Walker dies at 64; pioneer in X-ray optics], ''Stanford Report'' (May 2, 2001).</ref>  Walker was survived by his second wife Victoria, a daughter, Heather M. M. Walker; two stepsons, Nigel D. Gibbs and Eric D. Gibbs; and four grandchildren.<ref name=nytimes_20010509/>

In 2016, the [[Astronomical Society of the Pacific]] instituted an annual Arthur B.C. Walker II Award "established to honor an outstanding scientist whose research and educational efforts substantially contributes to astronomy and who has (1) demonstrated a substantial commitment to mentoring students from [[underrepresented groups]] pursuing degrees in astronomy and/or (2) been instrumental in creating or supporting innovative and successful STEM programs designed to support underrepresented students or their teachers"; included is a scholarship to a student of the recipient's choice.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Katherine Johnson to receive the ASP's new Arthur B.C. Walker II Award|url=https://www.astrosociety.org/society-news/katherine-johnson-to-receive-the-asps-new-arthur-b-c-walker-ii-award/|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161016173149/https://www.astrosociety.org/society-news/katherine-johnson-to-receive-the-asps-new-arthur-b-c-walker-ii-award/|archive-date=October 16, 2016|website=Astronomical Society of the Pacific}}</ref>
